In C#, an interface allows multiple different classes or structs to be treated as the

or read the value from JSON).

Unity 2D has two methods of dealing with depth sorting:

each card.

Implementing Game Logic
Let's start by delineating the possible actions that can happen in the game:
A. A card can move from the draw pile to become the target card.
B. A card in the mine that is ranked one higher or one lower than the target card
can move from the mine to become the target card (Ace and King wrap around,
so if the target card is an Ace, either or 2 or a King may be played on it).
C. If the target card is replaced by any other card, the replaced target card then
moves to the discard pile.
D. If a face-down card has no more cards hiding it, it becomes face-up.
E. Either of two conditions can cause the game to be over:
■ The player wins because the mine is empty
■ The player loses because the draw pile is empty and there are no more pos-

ALWAYS TRY TO FIND EFFICIENT WAYS TO TEST VARIOUS GAME
CONDITIONS As an example of not doing this well, I have frequently seen
students play through an entire level of a game to test the boss battle at
the end of the level, make a small tweak to some settings, and then play
through the entire level again to test the boss battle again. Please remem-
ber that your time is your most precious resource and act accordingly. In that
example, the students should have created a separate test scene with just
the boss battle to do all their tweaking and then—only after the tweaking
was complete—should they have tested the boss within the context of the
larger level.
As an example of the right way to do this, when Jenova Chen and the team
at thatgamecompany were developing their latest game, Sky, they included
in each test build a hidden menu that allowed them to load one of many
locations in any level of the game and configure their player with any of the
abilities, clothing, and so on that a player could eventually find in the game.
This way, they could easily test any situation across their entire game with
(admittedly several) menu selections.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
addItIonal PROSPECTOR Game elements 975
Another example of doing this correctly was testing combat bugs in my
graduate school team's game Skyrates. Every once in a while, a player of
the game would run into a bizarre bug in combat that we had never seen. I
enabled any player to export an encrypted CombatData file that included all
the configuration data for the combat and then email that to us. Using these
CombatData files, we were able to recreate and resolve some extremely rare
bugs that we would never have encountered in the amount of testing that
our small team was able to do ourselves.
When you're creating your games, always think about how to make testing
easier and faster. Implementing ways for your team to load any situation
in the game and ways for your players to easily report rare bugs will take a
little up-front time but will always pay dividends later.
With a short game like Prospector, you don't need to do anything like make
a specific shuffle of cards that's always winnable, but it does help to think
about the shortest way to test wins and losses (e.g., emptying the draw pile
as quickly as possible to test a loss), and you should always try to keep rapid
testing in mind throughout your game development.
Next up, it's time to add some scoring.
Adding Scoring to Prospector
The original card game of Tri-Peaks, on which Prospector is based, has no scoring mecha-
nism beyond the player winning or losing. But as a digital game, it's really helpful to
keep score, make the scoring interesting, and maintain a high score so that players have

Earning Points in the Game
We will implement several ways to earn points in Prospector:
A. Moving a card from the mine to the target card earns 1 point.
B. Every subsequent card removed from the mine without drawing from the draw pile
increases the points awarded per card by 1, so a run of five cards from the mine
without a draw would be worth 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 points, respectively, for a total of 15
points for the run (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15).
C. If the player wins the round, they carry their score on to the next round. Whenever a
round is lost, their score for all rounds is totaled and checked against the high score
list.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

D. Silver cards: A silver card counts as two regular cards in a run. So, if the fourth
card in a run is a silver card, it will count as both the fourth and fifth cards in the run
(scoring first 4 points and then 5 points for it). The next card will count as the sixth
card in the run (scoring 6 points).
E. Gold cards: Each gold card in a run will increase a multiplier on the score by one.
A regular run with zero gold cards has a multiplier of one. If one of the cards in the
example run from point B were gold, then the multiplier would increase to 2, and
the run would be worth 30 points (15 x 2 = 30). If two cards in the run were gold,
then the multiplier would be 3, and the run would be worth 45 points (15 x 3 = 45).
The scoring will be handled by the Prospector class because it is aware of all the condi-
tions that could contribute to the score. We will also create a script named ScoreBoard to
handle all the visual elements of showing the score to the player.
We'll implement letters A through C in this chapter, and I'll leave letters D and E for you
to implement on your own later.

run with gold cards), it makes sense to store the score for the run separately and then

card from the drawPile).

The Prospector Background Image
One of the first things we can do to really make this game pop is to add a background
image. In the Materials folder that you imported at the beginning of the project are a
PNG named ProspectorBackground and a material named Mat_ProspectorBackground.
These are already set up for you, because you learned how to do so in previous
chapters.
Putting the Background Image On Screen
We need to place this image on screen and make it fit the camera as perfectly as
possible.
1. Make sure that the Projection of the Camera component of _MainCamera is set to
Orthographic and its Size is set to 10.
2. In Unity, add a quad to the scene (GameObject > 3D Object > Quad).
You could certainly have done the background image with a sprite, but I wanted to
show you how the sprites you have interact with a quad, which is a 3D version of a flat
image object.
3. Rename the quad ProspectorBackground and set its transform as follows:
ProspectorBackground (Quad) P:[ 0, 0, 10 ] R:[ 0, 0, 0 ] S:[ 26.667, 20, 1 ]
4. Drag the ProspectorBackground Mat from the Materials folder onto the quad.
Because _MainCamera's orthographicSi]e is 10, that means that there is a distance
of 10 units between the center of the screen and the nearest edge (which in this case
is the top and bottom), for a total height of 20 units visible on screen. The Prospector-
Background quad is 20 units high (Scale Y) because of this. And, because the screen is
at a 4:3 aspect ratio, 20 / 3 * 4 = 26.667 is the width (Scale X) that we need to set the
background to.

Image Compression Trade-offs
The background imported into your project with the most basic Image Import settings,
but there is a lot of room in Unity for tweaking and improving these settings. If you use
your mouse scroll wheel on the Game pane, you can zoom in to see some issues with
the image compression (particularly visible if you zoom in on the prospector's arm).
1. Open the Materials folder in the Project pane and select the ProspectorBackground
image. This shows the Texture2D import settings for that image in the Inspector.
2. To be able to see the compression issues best, set the Filter Mode to Point (no filter)
and click Apply. This removes the automatic blurring that Unity does on images.
3. Near the bottom of the Prospector Background Import Inspector, set Compression to
None, and then click the Apply button.
The image now looks great—even when zoomed in—but if you look at the image pre-
view at the bottom of the Inspector, you can see that the image is now 3.0MB in size,
which is pretty big for something that is targeting an online WebGL build. (If you don't
see an image preview, click the word "ProspectorBackground" on the bar at the bottom
of the Inspector.)
You may wonder how Unity's version of this image with "None" compression is 3.0MB,
when the original PNG file on your hard drive is exactly the same quality but is only
626KB (≈0.6MB). Unfortunately, Unity cannot use PNG compression, which originally
compressed this image at perfect quality in 626KB because while PNG compression is
lossless, it is not fast. So, you will need to make compression trade-offs between image
quality and size throughout your Unity projects.
4. Set Compression back to Normal Quality and click the Apply button. This shrinks the
ProspectorBackground file size down to about 0.8MB. However, there are still some
things we can do here.

of Goo) was the first person to call juice. A game is juicy if it is overly reactive to input. In
the real world, a concrete wall is not juicy, whereas gelatin is. If you poke the concrete
wall with your finger, it just sits there…nothing happens. On the other hand, when you
poke gelatin, it jiggles and glimmers, seeming to bounce with more energy than your
original poke. The bouncy, Bézier-based movement of the score makes it feel like more is
happening in the game than when we were just spitting out console messages.
5
The score movement in this game also serves another purpose: It helps your players
understand where the score is coming from and helps reveal the mechanics of the game
to them through play (rather than requiring them to read instructions).

Purho that you can watch at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fy0aCDmgnxg — accessed

takes the longest, and it can take a long time. In previous versions of Unity, it could take
as long as 30 minutes, though that is rarely the case now. Regardless, you will spend a
lot of time looking at the progress bar for the WebGL build (the longest time for me is
on the Compile WebAssembly module step). You might wonder what's taking so long.
Unity's WebGL process is pretty complex:
■ The C# you write in Visual Studio is converted into Intermediate Language (IL), low-
level compiled .NET bytecode generated by Visual Studio and other compilers.
■ This Intermediate Language is run through IL2CPP, which converts it from Intermedi-
ate Language to C++ (the CPP in the name). Unity uses IL2CPP for many of its build
platforms.
■ The C++ output from IL2CPP is run through Emscripten, which converts it to
WebAssembly (a.k.a. Wasm), JavaScript that is designed to be relatively small and
efficient (well, small and efficient for JavaScript).
This whole process takes a while; in fact, it's probably still happening for you. Might be
a good time to go get a coffee (or check out an Appendix B topic that you haven't yet
read).
After the build process completes, you may see a notification from your operating
system about something called Node.js attempting to access the Internet. This is okay
and is something that you should allow. As mentioned in Appendix A, when you choose
Build and Run, Unity launches a temporary web server to serve your WebGL project to
your web browser. That temporary web server is built on Node.js (a JavaScript-based
server programming language), and it wants to access the Internet.
If you later try to open the index.html file in your folder directly on your hard drive, the
WebGL won't load properly. As of the end of 2021, it seems impossible to run WebGL
builds directly from your hard drive except when you choose Build and Run from the
Unity File menu. To play your game, you can either choose Build and Run, or you can
upload the WebGL build (including the index.html file, the Build folder, and the Tem-
plateData folder) to a web server and play the build online.
